subjective.question: Define project management.
subjective.answer: Project management is the application of knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to project activities in order to meet or exceed stakeholder needs and expectations from a project. It involves balancing the competing demands of scope, time, cost, quality, resources and risk.

subjective.question: Define a software process.
subjective.answer: A software process is a set of activities whose goal is the development or evolution of software. It provides the framework of tasks, milestones and deliverables within which software is engineered, and it defines who does what, when it is done, and how the work is checked.

subjective.question: What are the characteristics (dimensions) of a project?
subjective.answer: A project is: (1) Temporary - it has a definite beginning and a definite end; (2) Unique - it produces a product, service or result that is different in some way from existing ones; (3) Aims - it is undertaken to achieve specific goals and objectives; (4) People - it is performed by people working in teams; and (5) Process - it progresses through a planned series of activities and phases (its life cycle).

subjective.question: Differentiate between a project, a program and routine activities.
subjective.answer: A project is a temporary and unique undertaking with a definite start and end, e.g. construction of a motorway. A program is a group of related projects managed in a coordinated way to obtain benefits not available from managing them individually; a program is longer in duration than its projects, e.g. provision of a faster, safe and international-standard traffic facility in Pakistan. Routine activities are ongoing, repetitive operations with no definite end, e.g. controlling the traffic flow of a city.

subjective.question: Name the players in the software process and explain their roles.
subjective.answer: There are five players: (1) Senior managers, who define the business issues that influence the project; (2) Project (technical) managers, who plan, motivate, organize and control the practitioners; (3) Practitioners, who provide the technical skills needed to engineer the product; (4) Customers, who specify the requirements for the software; and (5) End users, who interact with the software once it is released for production use.

subjective.question: What are the software engineering layers?
subjective.answer: Software engineering is a layered technology. The foundation is a total quality focus. Above it lies the process layer, which holds the framework of key process areas for effective delivery of software engineering technology. Next are the methods, which provide the technical how-to's for building software, and finally the tools, which provide automated or semi-automated support for the process and the methods.

subjective.question: Name the inputs of the Initiating Process.
subjective.answer: The inputs of the Initiating Process are: (1) Product Description, (2) Strategic Plan, (3) Selection Criteria, and (4) Historical Information.

subjective.question: What are the outputs of the Initiating Process?
subjective.answer: The outputs of the Initiating Process are: (1) Project Charter, (2) Project Manager assignments, (3) Constraints, and (4) Assumptions.

subjective.question: List the tasks performed in the Planning Process.
subjective.answer: The planning tasks include: scope planning, scope determination (definition), activity definition, activity sequencing, activity duration estimating, schedule development, resource planning, cost estimating, cost budgeting, risk management planning, quality planning, organizational planning, staff acquisition (resource allocation), communications planning, and procurement planning. A detailed project plan is produced during this process.

subjective.question: What are the tasks of the Executing Process?
subjective.answer: The executing process tasks are: (1) Project Plan Execution, (2) Quality Assurance, (3) Team Development, (4) Information Distribution, (5) Solicitation, (6) Source Selection, and (7) Contract Administration.

subjective.question: What are the tasks of the Controlling Process?
subjective.answer: The controlling process includes: overall (integrated) change control, scope verification and scope change control, schedule control, cost control, quality control, performance reporting, and risk monitoring and control. Its purpose is to measure progress regularly, identify variances from the plan, and take corrective action when necessary.

subjective.question: Do the project management process groups occur one after another without overlap? Explain.
subjective.answer: No. The five process groups - Initiating, Planning, Executing, Controlling and Closing - are not discrete, one-time events; they overlap and interact with each other throughout the project life cycle. For example, planning continues while execution is in progress, and controlling runs alongside execution from start to finish. The level of intensity of each group varies from phase to phase.

subjective.question: What is SMARTER? Also differentiate between goals and objectives.
subjective.answer: Objectives should be SMARTER: Specific, Measurable, Acceptable, Realistic, Time frame (bound by a time frame), Extending, and Rewarding. A goal is a broad, long-term statement of what is to be achieved - the aim or purpose of the effort. Objectives are the concrete, measurable steps that lead to the goal; unlike goals, objectives must be specific and measurable so that their achievement can be verified.

subjective.question: What is a formal change process? Why is it needed?
subjective.answer: A formal change process is a defined procedure through which every requested change to the project scope, requirements or baselines is documented, evaluated for its impact on cost, schedule and quality, approved or rejected by the authorized body (such as a change control board), and only then implemented and communicated. It is needed so that uncontrolled changes (scope creep) do not destroy the project plan, budget and quality.

subjective.question: What are the tasks of the product implementation phase?
subjective.answer: Product implementation includes: (1) Implementation plan creation - it defines the duration of implementation and the hardware and software prerequisites for implementing the product; (2) Support plan creation - covering the post-implementation support activities provided to the customer; (3) Training plan creation - for training the users of the product; and (4) User acceptance plan - whose primary focus is to ensure that the final software product offers all the functionality and performance that the customer wanted.

subjective.question: Differentiate between a leader and a manager.
subjective.answer: Leadership is path finding, while management is path following. A leader develops a vision of the future and strategies for achieving that vision, communicates the vision so that others understand and agree with it, and motivates and inspires people towards goal attainment. A manager, on the other hand, works within the existing structure: planning, organizing, staffing, directing, monitoring and controlling the work so that the defined goals are achieved efficiently.

subjective.question: Identify whether the following are tasks of a leader or a manager: (i) communicates vision, (ii) writes / is in charge of the project plan, (iii) motivates and inspires, (iv) influences people.
subjective.answer: Communicates vision, motivates and inspires, and influences people are tasks of a leader. Writing and being in charge of the project plan is a task of the manager (project manager), because it belongs to planning and organizing the work rather than to setting the direction.

subjective.question: What are people-related problems in software projects?
subjective.answer: People-related problems include: low motivation, problem employees, unproductive work environments, inefficient project management style, lack of stakeholder interest, friction among team members, and failure of managers to get things done. These problems arise from the human side of the project rather than from the product or the technology.

subjective.question: What are technology-related problems in software projects? What is the effect of switching tools in the middle of a project?
subjective.answer: Technology-related problems include: technology changes, switching of tools in the middle of the project, overestimated savings and benefits, integrating cross-platform products, and research-oriented development pressures. Switching tools mid-way is harmful because the team must spend time and effort learning the new tool, work in progress may have to be converted or redone, productivity drops during the transition, and the schedule slips.

subjective.question: What is the 80/20 rule (Pareto principle) in software projects?
subjective.answer: The 80/20 rule states that roughly 80% of the effects come from 20% of the causes. In software projects it is observed, for example, that about 20% of the modules contain 80% of the errors, 20% of the components consume 80% of the resources, and 20% of the effort produces 80% of the results. Managers therefore focus attention and quality effort on the vital few components.

subjective.question: What are the methods of requirement elicitation for developing an examination system for a university? Explain briefly.
subjective.answer: The suitable methods are: (1) Interviews - with the controller of examinations, teachers and students to learn the rules for paper setting, marking and result preparation; (2) Questionnaires - to collect requirements from a large number of students and faculty members; (3) FAST meetings - joint sessions of developers and university staff to agree on the requirements; (4) Observation - watching the existing manual examination process; and (5) Document analysis - studying existing result sheets, date sheets and examination rules. Combining these methods gives complete and consistent requirements.

subjective.question: What are context-free questions in requirements elicitation? Give examples.
subjective.answer: Context-free questions are questions that do not suggest any particular solution and can be asked in any context at the start of elicitation; they help establish the overall scope and goals of the system. Examples: Who is the user of the system? Who will maintain it? What problem will this product solve? What is the expected benefit of a good solution? Where else can a solution to this problem be obtained?

subjective.question: Discuss the effect of incomplete, inconsistent and ambiguous specifications on a software project.
subjective.answer: Incomplete specifications leave out required functionality, so features are discovered late and added at high cost. Inconsistent specifications contain contradictions, so different developers implement different behaviour and integration problems appear. Ambiguous specifications can be interpreted in more than one way, so the delivered product may not be what the customer meant. Together they cause rework, schedule delays, cost overruns, disputes with the customer and poor quality; this is why specification review and validation are essential.

subjective.question: What are FAST guidelines and goals?
subjective.answer: FAST (Facilitated Application Specification Technique) is a team-oriented approach to requirements gathering. Its goals are: to encourage the creation of a joint team of customers and developers, to identify the problem and propose elements of the solution, to negotiate different approaches, and to specify a preliminary set of requirements. Its guidelines include: the meeting is held at a neutral site, a facilitator controls the meeting, an agenda is set and followed, preparation is done before the meeting, and the meeting is attended by both software engineers and customers.

subjective.question: What is a Preliminary User Manual? Why is it developed during requirements analysis?
subjective.answer: A Preliminary User Manual is a document written during the requirements phase as if the software product already existed, describing the system from the user's point of view - its functions, screens and usage - before the system is designed. It is developed because writing it forces the analyst and the customer to think through the system's behaviour concretely, exposes missing or unclear requirements early, and gives the customer something tangible to review and approve.

subjective.question: How does requirements analysis bridge the gap between system engineering and software design?
subjective.answer: System engineering identifies the overall role of software in the larger system and produces system-level requirements. Requirements analysis refines and models these requirements: the problem is recognized, solutions are evaluated and synthesized, the requirements are modeled and specified in the Software Requirements Specification, and the specification is reviewed. The resulting analysis model serves as the foundation for software design, so requirements analysis forms the bridge between system-level requirements engineering and software design.

subjective.question: What are the major design styles?
subjective.answer: The major design styles are: (1) Object-oriented design - the system is organized around objects and classes; (2) Structured design - the system is decomposed into functions and procedures using structured techniques; and (3) Data-structured design - the design is derived from the structure of the data the system processes.

subjective.question: What are the design attributes (characteristics) that a design must describe?
subjective.answer: A software design must describe four attributes: (1) Data structure - the organization of the data used by the system; (2) Software architecture - the overall structure of the components and their relationships; (3) Interface representations - the interfaces between components and with external systems and users; and (4) Procedural detail - the algorithmic detail of each component.

subjective.question: Differentiate between the Waterfall model and the Spiral model.
subjective.answer: The Waterfall model is a linear, sequential model in which each phase (requirements, design, implementation, testing, maintenance) is completed before the next begins; it suits projects with clear, stable requirements. The Spiral model is a risk-driven, iterative model that combines prototyping with systematic development; each loop of the spiral includes risk analysis, so it suits large, complex and high-risk projects where requirements may evolve.

subjective.question: Which SDLC model would you select for a banking system? Justify your choice.
subjective.answer: For a banking system the Waterfall model is appropriate. Banking requirements (accounts, transactions, security and regulatory rules) are well understood, stable and must be completely specified before implementation; the system demands very high reliability and correctness, which the disciplined, document-driven waterfall process supports. Late changes are rare and costly, so a sequential model with thorough early specification and review is the safest choice.

subjective.question: Which SDLC model would you select for a satellite (space) system? Justify your choice.
subjective.answer: For a satellite system the Spiral model is appropriate. Such a system is large, complex, expensive and high-risk, with severe constraints and little room for failure; the spiral model's repeated cycles of planning, risk analysis, engineering and evaluation allow risks to be identified and resolved early, prototypes to be evaluated, and the design to be refined before full commitment of resources.

subjective.question: What does the code generation step perform?
subjective.answer: The code generation step translates the design of the software into a machine-readable form. In the traditional view, this step produces source code in a programming language that directly reflects the procedural and structural detail created during design.

subjective.question: What are McCall's software quality factors?
subjective.answer: McCall classified quality factors into three categories. Product Operation: Correctness, Reliability, Efficiency, Integrity, Usability. Product Revision: Maintainability, Flexibility, Testability. Product Transition: Portability, Reusability, Interoperability, Configurability, Expandability.

subjective.question: What is the importance of software review?
subjective.answer: Software reviews (including formal technical reviews, inspections and walkthroughs) detect errors and defects early, before they are propagated into later phases where fixing them is far more expensive. They improve quality, verify that standards and procedures are followed, provide a basis for process improvement, and help the team share understanding of the product. A review of the Software Requirements Specification, for example, is conducted by both the software developer and the customer before sign-off.

subjective.question: Differentiate between a bibliography and an appendix in a software specification.
subjective.answer: A bibliography is the list of all documents, standards and references cited in or used for preparing the specification. An appendix contains supplementary material that supports the specification but is not part of its main body, such as detailed tables, formats or supporting data. Finally, a specification includes both a bibliography and an appendix.

subjective.question: What are the activities of Software Configuration Management (SCM)?
subjective.answer: The SCM activities are: (1) Identifying Objects - identifying the software configuration items (documents, code, data) to be controlled; (2) Controlling Versions - managing the different versions of configuration objects created during the process; (3) Controlling Changes - controlling how changes to configuration items are requested, evaluated, approved and made; (4) Auditing Configuration - verifying that the configuration is complete and consistent; and (5) Communicating Changes - reporting and communicating the changes to all concerned parties.

subjective.question: Differentiate between Software Configuration Management (SCM) and Software Maintenance.
subjective.answer: SCM is concerned with identifying, controlling and tracking the versions and changes of all software work products throughout development; it manages the integrity of the evolving product and its baselines. Software maintenance is the activity performed after the software is delivered and in use, to correct faults, improve performance or adapt the product to a changed environment. SCM supports maintenance by ensuring that every change made during maintenance is controlled, recorded and applied to the correct version.

subjective.question: Name any configuration control tools.
subjective.answer: Configuration control is supported by version control tools that combine procedures and tools to manage the different versions of configuration objects, for example: CVS, Subversion (SVN), Git, Microsoft Visual SourceSafe, and Rational ClearCase. Their check-in and check-out facilities provide synchronization control, ensuring that parallel changes made by two different people do not overwrite one another.

subjective.question: What is a prototype? When is prototyping used?
subjective.answer: A prototype is an early, working version of the software (or part of it) built quickly to demonstrate concepts and clarify requirements. Prototyping (rapid prototyping) is particularly helpful in projects where the requirements are difficult to specify in advance: the customer evaluates the prototype, gives feedback, and the requirements are refined before full-scale development.

subjective.question: What is the effect of incorrect or incomplete requirements on a software project?
subjective.answer: Incorrect or incomplete requirements are discovered late, usually during design, coding or after delivery, when correction is most expensive. They lead to rework, schedule delays, cost overruns, a product that does not satisfy the customer, and in severe cases complete project failure. This is why requirements must be gathered through a proper elicitation process and reviewed before design begins.
